description: We are Stellar Pyros, a student team driven by space, technology, and design. Combining our strengths in UX/UI, research, and technical problem-solving, we turn big ideas into practical solutions. For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we leverage open data to tackle a real-world issue. We want to challenge ourselves, build an engaging prototype, and create something meaningful we can be proud of.
summary:
IGNITE-AI is an open-source (Apache-2.0) fire-safety analytics tool for spacecraft. It predicts whether a flame will spread over a spacecraft material under given oxygen, pressure, airflow, and gravity conditions, and it uses only published NASA experiments. The tool includes a 3D flame simulator for Earth, Moon, Mars, ISS, and transit-cabin environments, a prediction page showing the nearest real experiments with verbatim quotes, and a question-answering assistant grounded in a NASA combustion knowledge base with citations. It is trained on 143 real flame-spread tests from 13 NASA reports across four gravity levels (0, 0.165, 0.38, and 1 g). Cross-validated accuracy is 0.734 against a 0.608 majority baseline.
Fire behaves very differently in microgravity: flames are rounded, can be nearly invisible, and can persist as cool flames, which makes intuition from Earth unreliable. IGNITE-AI addresses this by refusing to predict outside the conditions that were actually tested, so it can't extrapolate beyond the data. It also shows its evidence and publishes an honest model card. This transparency matters for crew safety on space stations and during rocket transit, where trust in a prediction depends on seeing its sources.
details: How it works IGNITE-AI predicts whether a flame will spread over a spacecraft material given oxygen concentration, pressure, airflow, and gravity. The model is trained on 143 flame-spread experiments from 13 NASA reports, covering 0, 0.165 (Moon), 0.38 (Mars), and 1 g. A range guard blocks predictions outside the tested conditions. For each prediction, the tool shows the decision boundary over the real NASA tests and the nearest actual experiments, with verbatim quotes. A local Q&A assistant answers from a knowledge base of 24 NASA combustion investigations. Every answer is a quoted passage with a source link, so it can't invent facts. A 3D flame simulator lets users change oxygen, pressure, and airflow for Earth, Moon, Mars, ISS, and transit-cabin environments. A Safety Measures page covers detection, ventilation shutdown, suppression, material selection, and crew procedures. An open API is also available. Benefits and intended impact Gives mission planners, students, and researchers a fast, transparent way to explore microgravity fire risk. Builds trust through honesty: it refuses to extrapolate, publishes its model card (cross-validated accuracy of 0.734 vs. a 0.608 baseline, with per-gravity accuracy and a confusion matrix), and cites every source. Makes NASA's scattered combustion research accessible to the public. Supports safer material selection and crew awareness for space station orbit and rocket transit. Tools and technology The project is open source (Apache-2.0) on GitHub and hosted on Netlify. It has an interactive web front end with a 3D simulator, a machine-learning classifier, a retrieval-based Q&A system, and a documented API. [Add your specific languages, libraries, and frameworks here, such as Python, scikit-learn, or Three.js. I couldn't verify these from the site.] Creativity Most AI tools aim to always give an answer. IGNITE-AI is designed to know its limits. It combines prediction, evidence, and visualization in one place, and its extractive Q&A (quotes only, no generation) suits a safety-critical field. Factors considered Data scarcity: only four gravity levels have data, so the tool is explicit about what it can and can't say. Safety and trust: the range guard, verbatim citations, and honest accuracy reporting. Accessibility: it works for non-experts, and a plain-text summary and API are provided. Responsible AI use: an AI-use disclosure and a note that NASA does not endorse the project.
